title: terminate called without an active exception terminate called recursively terminate called recursively
body: Our Qdrant service had been running normally, but now every restart logs "terminate called without an active exception" and "terminate called recursively." Docker reports the container as running, but ports 6333, 6334, and 6335 refuse connections, so reads, writes, and the dashboard are unavailable. We have 33 collections. Memory usage was high, but doubling the available memory did not restore the service. I need to understand the cause and get the service back to normal.

symptoms_visible: Every restart logs "terminate called without an active exception" followed by "terminate called recursively."
Docker reports the container as running, but connections to ports 6333, 6334, and 6335 are refused, so I cannot read, write, or access the dashboard.
I doubled the available memory, but the same behavior remained.
N0.label: N0 recursive termination and refused ports reported

symptoms_visible: After expanding the memory, it is not exhausted during startup, but Qdrant still logs the recursive termination messages and its ports remain inaccessible.
N1.label: N1 startup memory exhaustion checked

symptoms_visible: The affected three-machine deployment still refuses connections after restart, while I cannot reproduce the behavior on a small new cluster.
N2.label: N2 affected deployment characterized

symptoms_visible: On the rebuilt Qdrant 1.9.1 cluster, shards became dead or partial during the data import.
Restarting after the shard degradation again produced "terminate called recursively."
N3_x.label: N3_x upgrade aftermath

symptoms_visible: After merging the 33 collections into one multi-tenant collection, shard problems still occurred when I wrote a large amount of data.
N4_x.label: N4_x collection consolidation aftermath

symptoms_visible: With parallel batches of 1,000 points and about 5,000 to 10,000 points written each second overnight, shards became dead or partial; restarting afterward produced the recursive termination error.
The same sequence occurred on the one-collection deployment during the large import.
N5.label: N5 high-volume reproduction documented

symptoms_visible: After I limited the write rate, the cluster remained available and everything looked fine.
The problem had still occurred with one collection under large writes; reducing the write rate is what stopped it from recurring.
N_terminal.label: terminal stable after write throttling

question_patterns: Can you monitor memory while Qdrant starts and confirm whether the machine or container actually runs out of memory?
After increasing the memory limit, what does memory usage look like during startup?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I checked during startup. After expanding the memory, it was not exhausted, but the result was still the same.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The container reaches its memory limit during every startup and is killed by the operating system.
Memory is high during startup but remains below the expanded limit, and the same termination messages appear.

edges.comment: Reporter c6 answers maintainer c4 about the reporter's affected deployment. The measurement rules out simple startup memory exhaustion after the earlier memory expansion, but does not prove the eventual trigger.

question_patterns: Which Qdrant version is the affected cluster running?
What image tag is configured in Docker Compose?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The affected compose file uses qdrant/qdrant:v1.6.0.

question_patterns: Can you describe the cluster topology where this occurs?
How many machines and shards are involved in the affected deployment?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I am using three machines for sharding.

question_patterns: Approximately how much data is stored on each machine?
What is the data volume of the affected deployment?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The data volume on a single machine is approximately 429 G.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The cluster is empty and the same crash occurs immediately after creating the first collection.

question_patterns: Can you provide the Docker Compose and production configuration used by the affected cluster?
Please share a reduced test case or, if that is not possible, the version and configuration.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I cannot reproduce it on the smallest new cluster, but I can provide the affected data volume, version, compose file, and production configuration. The compose enables clustering, exposes ports 6333 through 6335, and mounts the storage, snapshots, and production config paths.

question_patterns: Can you simplify this into a small reproducer?
Does the problem also happen on a small new cluster?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: There is no way for me to reproduce it on the smallest new cluster.

edges.comment: Reporter c7 answers maintainer c5 with the reporter's own topology, version, data volume, compose file, and configuration. No other participant's deployment is folded into this chain.

solution.intent: Upgrade and rebuild the affected cluster on the current Qdrant version in case the old 1.6.0 build is responsible for the restart failure.
solution.concrete_example: Rebuild the three-machine cluster with Qdrant 1.9.1 and re-import the data, then check whether the shard and restart failures recur.

edges.comment: Reporter c8 asks about upgrading; maintainer c9 says an upgrade is possible but is not expected to solve the situation. Reporter c12-c15 and c18 then describes rebuilding the same three-machine deployment on 1.9.1, after which shard dead/partial states and the recursive restart failure recur. Upgrade alone is therefore falsified.

solution.intent: Replace the 33-collection layout with one multi-tenant collection to avoid the collection-per-partition usage pattern suspected of causing the failure.
solution.concrete_example: Consolidate the 33 collections into one collection and partition tenants using payload-based multi-tenancy, then repeat the import.

edges.comment: Maintainer c9 recommends a different multi-tenancy layout based on an assumption of many collections. Reporter c10-c12 explains there were 33 multi-tenant collections and tries one collection; reporter c26 states that the same problem still occurs with one collection when writes are large. Collection consolidation is useful guidance but not the fix for this incident.

question_patterns: What exact import pattern reproduces the shard failure?
How large are the batches, and how many writes do you issue in parallel?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I write batches of 1,000 points to the three machines, with about five to ten batches running in parallel.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: No import is running; the shards become dead on an idle cluster immediately after creation.
I use batches of 500 instead of 1,000 but reach approximately the same total sustained write rate.

question_patterns: Approximately how many points per second are written when the problem develops?
What sustained write throughput do you observe during the overnight run?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Approximately 5,000 to 10,000 points are written every second, and after running like that overnight the shards become dead or partial.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The failure occurs at one point per minute and is unrelated to an import or other load.

question_patterns: How much data does the backup import write over a longer interval?
Can you quantify the import volume per hour?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: During this backup import I wrote about 20 million vector records per hour, and it took more than ten hours to restore less than half of the data.

question_patterns: What happens immediately before the recursive termination appears?
Does the restart error occur before or after the shards enter dead or partial states?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The shard dead and shard partial states appear first. If they are not restored for a long time, restarting then causes "terminate called recursively."

counterfactual_candidates.answer: All shards remain healthy, and the recursive termination occurs before any data is written.

question_patterns: Can you share the collection creation parameters used in the reproducer?
What shard, replication, and write-consistency settings are configured?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The collection uses shard_number 3, replication_factor 3, and write_consistency_factor 2. I posted the full collection parameters along with my earlier configuration.

question_patterns: What is the vector size and payload shape of the imported records?
How large is each vector?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Each vector is 512 dimensions and has three payload parameters.

edges.comment: Reporter c15, c18-c20 provides the reproduction on the reporter's rebuilt deployment: parallel 1,000-point batches, observed throughput, overnight shard degradation, restart sequence, collection parameters, and vector shape. Maintainer c17 disputes the reporter's proposed concurrency mechanism, so the graph preserves the raw sequence rather than claiming that Qdrant's internal sharding collapsed.

solution.intent: Throttle sustained ingestion so the deployment does not return to the shard-degraded state, using bounded concurrency, retries, or a queue, and verify that shards, ports, and restarts remain healthy under the controlled workload.
solution.concrete_example: Reduce and bound the number of concurrent 1,000-point batches. If necessary, place imports behind a queue and retry transiently rejected writes rather than sustaining the previous ingest pressure. Monitor shard status, confirm ports 6333-6335 remain reachable, and perform a controlled restart before declaring the incident resolved.

edges.comment: Reporter c25-c26 confirms the resolution on the same deployment: memory was increased and 1.9.1 retained, but upgrade and collection consolidation were not independently effective; limiting the write rate is the change the reporter says completely stopped recurrence. The thread does not establish a deeper internal Qdrant mechanism, so the solution is scored as the empirically verified operational fix.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify sustained high-volume ingestion as the empirically demonstrated trigger in this deployment, grounded in the parallel-batch reproduction, shard dead/partial states, and the restart failure that followed; must not present the reporter's proposed internal sharding-collapse mechanism as proven.
Must recommend limiting or applying backpressure to the write rate, with bounded concurrency and optionally retries or a queue, as the operational fix that restored stability.
Must not treat increasing memory alone as the fix: memory was doubled and was not exhausted during startup, yet the failure remained.
Must not treat upgrading to Qdrant 1.9.1 or merging 33 collections into one as sufficient fixes: the issue recurred on 1.9.1 and with one collection under large writes.
Must ask the reporter to verify sustained shard health, reachable service ports, and a controlled restart under the limited write workload before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced infrastructure operator running a large three-machine Qdrant cluster; comfortable with Docker Compose, YAML configuration, collection parameters, sharding, replication, high-volume imports, and operational recovery, but relies on maintainers for Qdrant internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, detailed, and empirical; supplies full configurations and throughput figures, proposes causal theories, asks direct operational questions, and revises the deployment to test recommendations.
